paper.citation: Athey, S., Imbens, G. W. and Wager, S. (2018). Approximate residual balancing: Debiased inference of average treatment effects in high dimensions. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), 80(4), 597–623. DOI: 10.1111/rssb.12268.
paper.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology)
paper.source_locator: Section 5.2, unnumbered paragraph headed by the sparse two-stage setting, electronic-reprint PDF reader pp. 21–22/27 (zero-based indices 20–21), printed pp. 617–618; Table 3 and its footnote on printed p. 618 give n=1000, p=2000, rho=0.5, and 400 replications. The paragraph contains no numbered equations. Supplementary file is listed as proofs, but the publisher download returned HTTP 403 in this run. The paper cites the balanceHD R package, but no author-code commit was used or pinned.

mechanism.name: Sparse two-stage high-dimensional treatment assignment with Gaussian AR(1) covariates

generation_equations.label: Covariates
generation_equations.expression: X_i ~ Normal_p(0,Sigma), Sigma_jk=rho^|j-k|; Table 3 uses rho=0.5, p=2000.

generation_equations.label: Structure coefficient profile
generation_equations.expression: beta_Y,j proportional to 1/j^2 for j=1,...,p; Table 3 varies ||beta_Y||_2 in {1,4}.

generation_equations.label: Very-sparse-labeled propensity profile
generation_equations.expression: beta_W,j proportional to 1/j^2 for j=1,...,p; Table 3 varies ||beta_W||_2 in {1,4}. All coordinates are technically nonzero.

generation_equations.label: Dense propensity profile
generation_equations.expression: beta_W,j proportional to 1/sqrt(j) for j=1,...,p; Table 3 varies ||beta_W||_2 in {1,4}.

generation_equations.label: Noise
generation_equations.expression: epsilon_i1 and epsilon_i2 are independent standard Gaussian errors; implementation samples N(0,1) independently from X and across individuals as an explicit convention.

sampling.unit: Individual; reference experiment n=1000 and p=2000.
sampling.dependence: The implementation samples individuals independently. Within each individual, X coordinates are correlated with Cov(X_ij,X_ik)=rho^|j-k|; W depends on X and latent epsilon_1; Y depends on X, W and epsilon_2. No within-person repeated measures, clusters, panels or interference. Cross-independence beyond the paper's stated error independence is an implementation assumption recorded above.

assumptions: Consistency and well-defined treatment interventions W=0 and W=1.
No interference: one individual's potential outcomes do not depend on other individuals' treatment assignments.
Treatment exchangeability conditional on X under the implementation convention that epsilon_1 is independent of epsilon_2 and X; then W is independent of both potential outcomes conditional on X.

Pointwise positivity holds for finite X because the logistic probability is strictly between 0 and 1 after integrating over epsilon_1. Uniform overlap is not guaranteed on unbounded Gaussian support and is a scientific review item.
The outcome disturbance epsilon_2 is shared across the two potential outcomes for each individual; this potential-outcome coupling follows the structural observed-outcome equation.

properties.notes: p=2000 exceeds the reference n=1000. Both beta_Y_j proportional to j^-2 and beta_W_j profiles (j^-2 or j^-1/2) are nonzero for every j=1,...,p; effective_dimension is therefore 2000 under an exact-support definition, even though the paper calls the j^-2 propensity profile 'very sparse' and its signal is strongly concentrated in early coordinates. No interaction terms occur. The treatment assignment uses the nonlinear function 1/(1+exp(theta_i)); the outcome surface is linear.

estimand.name: ATE
estimand.definition: E[Y(1)-Y(0)] under interventions setting W=1 versus W=0 in the superpopulation defined by the sparse two-stage DGP; use the same pre-treatment X and epsilon_2 for both potential outcomes.

truth.expression: E[Y(1)-Y(0)] under interventions setting W=1 versus W=0 in the superpopulation defined by the sparse two-stage DGP; use the same pre-treatment X and epsilon_2 for both potential outcomes.
truth.derivation: Analytic structural contrast; Y_i(1)=X_i^T beta_Y+0.5+epsilon_i2 and Y_i(0)=X_i^T beta_Y+epsilon_i2, hence difference 0.5 exactly. estimated_error is zero because no numerical integration or simulation is used.

adaptations: Generate X from the specified Gaussian Toeplitz covariance using an AR(1) Gaussian recursion; this is distribution-equivalent to drawing a multivariate normal with Sigma_ij=rho^|i-j|, but not the same pseudorandom sequence.

Independently sample covariate rows and the two standard-normal errors. The source states that epsilon_i1 and epsilon_i2 are independent standard Gaussian, but does not enumerate every cross-independence relation with X and across i; this executable factorization is an explicit implementation convention pending scientific review.

State the benchmark target explicitly as population ATE. The paper's observed outcome equation has a constant additive treatment term 0.5, so its corresponding population ATE and ATT both equal 0.5 under the potential-outcome interpretation Y_i(w)=X_i^T beta_Y+0.5 w+epsilon_i2.
